title: Panel
definition:
Expandable content that appears over the viewer when you click “Learn more” or similar buttons. Panels provide additional context without leaving the current step.

Telar supports two layers of panels:
- **Layer 1**: Opens from the main step
- **Layer 2**: Opens from within layer 1

This progressive disclosure allows readers to choose their depth of engagement.

title: Step
definition:
One stop in a Telar story. The object fills the screen behind a text card. As the reader moves through the story, the view goes to the part of the object the step is about, and the card passes over it. For images, that part is set with `x`, `y`, and `zoom`; for video and audio, with a start and an end time.

Each step's card shows a question and a short answer, and the step can offer up to two panels with more detail.

title: Story
definition:
A sequence of steps that form a visual narrative. Each story appears as a separate entry in the project sheet and can be navigated independently.

In Telar, stories combine text and objects to build arguments, explore themes, or guide readers through visual material. The demo story you are viewing is an example of a story that teaches while it tells.

title: Viewer
definition:
The part of a Telar story that shows the object. It fills the whole screen, behind the text cards. For images it supports deep zoom and panning, so readers can look closely at every detail.

The viewer works with IIIF objects (hosted by museums and libraries) and self-hosted objects (from your own collection). Readers can zoom and pan freely; your coordinates set where the view goes at each step.

title: IIIF
definition:
IIIF (International Image Interoperability Framework) is an open standard that lets institutions share high-resolution images online. Museums, libraries, and archives publish IIIF manifests — structured URLs that describe an image and its metadata.

In Telar, paste a manifest URL into the source_url column of your objects tab and Telar handles the rest: zoom, pan, and deep-zoom all work automatically. This story uses both a self-hosted image (demo-leviathan) and an external IIIF manifest from Princeton (demo-atlas-allegory).

title: The Kogi loom
definition:
Among the Kogi of the Sierra Nevada of Santa Marta, a loom—in addition to being a tool for weaving—is a map that represents the human body and the geography of the Sierra.

The body of a man with his arms crossed forms the shape of the loom. In turn, the four corners of the loom represent the four cities of the lowlands (Santa Marta, Riohacha, Fundación, and Valledupar), while the crosses that shape the interior represent the mountain peaks.

![Framework of a Kogi loom [Marco de un telar Kogi]The Loom of Life: A Kogi Principle of Integration. G. Reichel-Dolmatoff, 1978](https://content.telar.org/assets/images/paisajes/1.3.3.1.jpg){md}
Framework of a Kogi loom [*Marco de un telar Kogi*] The Loom of Life: A Kogi Principle of Integration. G. Reichel-Dolmatoff, 1978.

The form of the loom creates a frame with which the Kogi conceptualize and represent geography and which can also be expressed on their bodies.

Reichel-Dolmatoff, G. (1978). The Loom of Life: A Kogi Principle of Integration. *Journal of Latin American Lore*, Volume 4 (Number 1).

title: Jorge Tadeo Lozano
definition:
Jorge Tadeo Lozano was born in Bogotá in 1771. He studied in Europe and became interested in natural history. This allowed him to join the Royal Botanical Expedition in New Granada in 1803 as the person in charge of the zoological project. Given his high social and economic status, Lozano owned numerous estates in different climates, which made collecting animals for his zoological work easier. He went on to write *The Fauna of Cundinamarca* and participated in the publication of *Correo curioso, erudito, económico y mercantil de la ciudad de Santa Fe de Bogotá*, one of the first enlightened journals of the Republic. His work was part of the Spanish Crown’s wider search for ways to promote colonial economies through scientific expeditions during the Enlightenment, specifically aiming to identify new products and commodities for export.

As part of his administrative duties within the Spanish empire, Lozano was named lieutenant protector of the Indigenous peoples of Bosa, Fusagasugá, and Usaquén in 1807. With the consolidation of the first government of the Republic, Lozano served as the first president of Cundinamarca and of the United Provinces of New Granada, only to be deposed in 1811 in a coup d’état led by Antonio Nariño. After the Reconquista, Pablo Morillo’s forces shot Lozano on July 6th, 1816 for his participation in republican politics in what is now the *Plaza de Los Mártires*.

title: On the reduction of “indios”
definition:
**Law One. *Indios* shall be reduced to villages.**

![Law One. Indios shall be reduced to villages](https://content.telar.org/assets/images/paisajes/2.2.1.jpg){md}

> With great care and attention, we have always tried to find appropriate means for ensuring that the  *indios* are instructed in the Holy Catholic Faith and Evangelical Law, and forget the errors of their former rites and ceremonies, and live in law and order, and to ensure that this was executed with precision, the members of our Council of the Indies met several times (…), and seeking to do right by God and by us, they resolved that the  *indios* should be reduced to settlements and avoid living separately and divided by ridges and mountains, depriving themselves of all spiritual benefits.

Libro VI, Título III. De las Reducciones y pueblos de *indios* (On Reductions and Indian Villages). Julián de Paredes, 1681. Courtesy of Biblioteca Nacional de España, Madrid. [See full document](../../objects/demo-obj27/)

title: “On the need for a church with a door and key in every reducción”
definition:
![Law iiij: On the need for a church with a door and key in every reducción.](https://content.telar.org/assets/images/paisajes/2.2.2.jpg){sm}

**Law iiij: On the need for a church with a door and key in every *reducción*.**

> “A church must be built in every *reducción*, even if the number of  *indios* is small, in which Mass can be said with decency, and it must have a door and key, even if it is subject to a parish and far away from it.”

Recopilación de Leyes de los Reinos de las Indias. Mandadas imprimir y publicar por la magestad católica del Rey don Carlos II. Libro VI, título III. Julián de Paredes, 1681. Courtesy of Biblioteca Nacional de España, Madrid. [See full document](../../objects/demo-obj27/)

title: Cacicazgo
definition: The Spanish began to use the terms “cacique” and “cacicazgo” in the islands of the Caribbean after they noticed that Indigenous peoples used these Arawak words to refer to their authorities. From then on, the Spanish used these as generic terms to refer to Indigenous authorities throughout the empire. The Muisca used the term *psihipqua* to designate some of these authorities. The *caciques* that led Muisca communities after the conquest had to change their forms of government in a colonial context in which Indigenous peoples were put under increasing pressure by imperial structures of governance. By the late sixteenth century, the historical record indicates that many *caciques* dressed as Spaniards, used the title “don” and a European name (like don Francisco de Ubaque), and financed murals, masses, and Catholic celebrations.

title: Don Francisco
definition:
> By the late sixteenth century, the cacique of Ubaque called himself don Francisco. Don Francisco saw himself as a Christian man. He dressed in a blue suit and a cape, a hat with feathers, and wore a sword at his waist. As he himself declared, his weapon and horse were always ready to confront an uprising of *indios*. In his home, the decorations, tables, and bed indicated that he ate and slept like any Spanish gentleman. He enjoyed reading and writing, attending mass, and living according to the values of the Catholic faith.

> In order to acquire his European outfits, don Francisco often found himself indebted to the merchants of Santafé, and even tried to sell the best farming lands of his community to his *encomendero* in order to cover his debts. In 1583, don Francisco appeared before the Royal Audiencia of Santafé with a petition to change the succession practices of Muisca cacicazgos. Don Francisco wanted King Philip II to decree that nephews could no longer inherit cacicazgos (as was the norm following the criteria of the matrilineal kinship groups prevalent in Muisca communities), but that sons should instead inherit (as was the case in Catholic societies). In his petition, don Francisco complained of his subjects’ idolatrous customs and stated that these needed to be altered; this stance lost him the support of his community.

> “I am married… according to the order of the Holy Mother Church, to Doña Beatríz, my wife, and our marriage gave us a legitimate child and we live like the Spanish do, politically and in their clothing, preserving what Christians preserve both in the spiritual and the earthly, by way of example to all other *indios* in this land.” — Don Francisco

> Don Francisco “is a clever speaker of our Spanish language, of very good manner and reason, so much so that in this whole Kingdom… this witness does not know another cacique like this one… He is friends with the Spanish and when they visit his village and quarters he hosts them and prays, setting a table in the manner of the Spanish and providing them with a refined meal, as if he truly was Spanish.” — Miguel de Espejo

> “The shrines and statuettes of the false gods his ancestors kept and worshipped, the said don Francisco has destroyed, broken, burned, and ruined.”

> “He has tried to imitate the good manners of the Spanish with such effort, that his very subjects the “indios” have been displeased by it saying that he does not practice the rites and ceremonies of the caciques of their ancestors.”

Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Audiencia de Santafé 125, n. 10. [See full document](../../objects/demo-obj25/)

title: On indigenous palisades
definition:
> “The forms of their houses and buildings, although they are made of wood and covered with a long hay that is found there, are of the strangest making and manner ever seen, especially those of the caciques and nobles, because they are like fortresses with many fences around them, in the way the Labyrinth of Troy is usually depicted here, [and] the houses have great courtyards with great sculptures and also paintings everywhere in it.”

Anonymous. “Epítome de la conquista del Nuevo Reino de Granada.”

title: On Indigenous peoples living in the city
definition:
> “Having understood the disorders and excesses seen in this city of Santafé de Bogotá due to male and female *indios*, mestizos, and mulattoes that are without a master to serve and, for this reason, are found idle and like vagabonds, which often results in grave damages and problems… I name him administrator of the said *indios* and mulatos.”

Courtesy of Archivo General de Indias (Sevilla), Audiencia de Santa Fe, L.93, n. 16 ff. 500r-501r. [See full document](../../objects/demo-obj44/)

title: On the distribution of encomiendas
definition:
**One. When the land is at peace, the Governor shall distribute the “indios” therein.**

![One. When the land is at peace, the Governor shall distribute the “indios” therein](https://content.telar.org/assets/images/paisajes/1.1.2.jpg){md}

> “Distribute the  *indios* among the settlers, so that each will take care of those allotted to him, and defend them, and protect them, providing a minister to instruct them in Christian doctrine and administer the Sacraments, keeping our Patronage, and teaching [them] to live in good order.”

Recopilación de Leyes de los Reinos de las Indias. Mandadas imprimir y publicar por la magestad católica del Rey don Carlos II. Libro VI, título VII. Julián de Paredes, 1681. Courtesy of Biblioteca Nacional de España, Madrid. [See full document](../../objects/demo-obj5/)

title: Pastures
definition: The grasslands represented in the *Painting* are probably not the same ones that cover the savanna today. In the eighteenth century, herders began importing African grass varieties that produced better grazing lands for cattle, though it is possible that these types of grasses had begun to spread in the New World previously since they were used for bedding on ships used in the slave trade.

title: Livestock
definition:
Cattle farming is part of a long process of coexistence between humans and animals known as “domestication.” Although domestication has traditionally been seen as a process in which humans dominated and tamed animals, recent research shows that this process was not fully controlled by humans and that many animals approached and coexisted with human societies of their own accord. In Africa and Eurasia, cattle farming has been practiced for at least 6,000 years, and in Spain, a livestock culture took shape throughout Antiquity and the Middle Ages as part of a network of trade and connection with other parts of Europe, the Middle East, and Asia. This form of livestock farming—centered on raising cows, sheep, goats, and pigs—depended on the use of horses and dogs to control freely-roaming livestock.

Indigenous societies in the New World had domesticated many animals, including dogs, turkeys, and ducks, which they used for food and in rituals, traded, and gave as tribute. In the Peruvian and Bolivian Andes, camelids, such as llamas and alpacas, were also raised and used as pack animals and for their wool. These were the only animals to be raised in large herds. When cows, pigs, and sheep were introduced into the New World after the Spanish invasion, they flourished quickly and adapted easily to an environment lacking in natural predators. Along with these came other unwanted species such as the Norway rat. Animal populations grew to such an extent that historian Elinor Melville has referred to the reproduction of ovine herds in Mesoamerica as “the plague of sheep.”

title: On the Indigenous diet
definition:
> “The foods of these peoples are the same as those in other places of the Indies plus some additional ones, as their main sustenance is maize and yucca, and apart from this they have two or three varieties of truffles they call *yomas* and one more similar to a turnip, which they call *cubias*. They put them in stews and they are of great sustenance. There is infinite salt because it is made there in the lands of Bogotá from caves containing salt from which they make great bricks of salt in huge quantities. These are then distributed to many places, especially through the Sierras of Opón and on to the Rio Grande, as was said. The meats the *indios* eat in this land are deer of which there are endless quantities, so abundant they can keep them here like we keep cattle. Likewise, they eat a species of animal similar to rabbits of which there is also a great number and which they call fucos and they are also found in Santa Marta and the seacoast where they are called *curies*.”

Anonymous, “Epítome de la conquista del Nuevo Reino de Granada”, p. 112, 1536.

title: On cattle in Indigenous lands
definition:
**Law X. The land farmed by *indios* shall be free of cattle.**

![Law X. The land farmed by indios shall be free of cattle](https://content.telar.org/assets/images/paisajes/3.3.1.jpg){md}

> “Our justice shall not allow cattle to enter lands farmed by *indios*, and it shall have any that enter them removed, imposing and enforcing grave penalties on those who defy it.”

Recopilación de Leyes de los Reinos de las Indias. Mandadas imprimir y publicar por la magestad católica del Rey don Carlos II. Libro IV, título XVII. Julián de Paredes, 1681. Courtesy of Biblioteca Nacional de España, Madrid. [See full document](../../objects/demo-obj47/)

title: Complaints regarding damages to crops caused by cattle
definition:
> “We come before you to state the troubles and destructions we have suffered in our town in the form of damage to our crops. There is a neighbor named Agustín Vela with over two hundred mules and horses, bovine livestock, and donkeys in our *resguardo*. Before we can harvest our pittance, which is wheat, maize, barley, and truffles, he brings in his tame and wild mules and destroys [our crops, he] has many lands starting on the Boyacá Bridge, where he has many grazing lands and can keep to his estate without maliciously fattening his mules with our grain by letting them into our crops every year with contempt for the poor because he is so rich and powerful, and ruining and diminishing us. And after we harvest and pile up our crops, he destroys them with his mules and livestock, and because we are poor and do not speak [Spanish], he is oppressing us. When we go to tell him, he says: “who measured the damages, who saw them?” and then he releases his dogs on us.”

Archivo General de la Nación, Resguardos-Boyacá, 7, D.10, ff. 672-704. 1672. [See full document](../../objects/demo-obj48/)

title: Lawsuit against Corregidores
definition:
> In 1594, an Indigenous authority from Pausaga expressed his non-conformity with the new demands regarding labor: “[indios no longer pay taxes] so they can pay the salary and the food of the *corregidor* (…), who provides them with no justice, and they would be better off saving what they pay the *corregidor* for the *demora* because they are too strained, and for paying the *quinto* [20% tax on metals and precious objects] to Our Lord the King, and they also have to comply with their general labor commitments which cause them great pains and many drown while crossing the rivers and others die while crossing the cold moors (*páramos*) and in Santafé they fall ill and many die due to the excessive work they are subjected to, and for trying to comply with these tasks, the *demoras*, and other fees they are forced to pay.”

Archivo General de la Nación/B, Colonia, *Visitas Cundinamarca*, t.8, f.381r-v. [See full document](../../objects/demo-obj51/)

title: Petition of Lorenzo de Requero
definition:
> “I, Lorenzo de Requero, was born in this court and due to my mother being a native of Ubatoque in the encomienda of Captain Antonio de Céspedes and relative of the caciques, in this jurisdiction I married Catalina Cimca, native of this village in which we have four children, and for their sustenance we have the *resguardos* Your Mercy mentioned, as well as lands in which we sow and grow food. These are lands we came to and acquired by natural right, and they are in the place called Quosvita, under and above it, and because I raise livestock and do what I have to do in my neighborhood, I fear the *encomendero*, or the cacique, or the *corregidor* will bother me, claiming that I am a mestizo and outside the boundary of the village where I am planting fruit trees to feed myself, and because I live doing no harm and the land belongs to my wife and my relatives and it is inside the *resguardo*.

> “I beg Your Mercy to give me assurance so that I am not bothered or disturbed because they want to expel me from the land as it belongs to my wife and my uncles and relatives, and in it I have my house and my home and I raise cattle and for this I sign,

> Lorenzo Requero.”

title: On vecinos in villages for “indios”
definition:
> “Another matter that alters the idea of enumeration is the doubt I expressed to Your Excellency in a letter dated 22nd August in the town of Paipa, on whether the sons of a non-native father or mother are in fact free from paying tribute, considering that pure *indios* are very rare, and it can be easily noted, with no further proof, that the species has degenerated; and so it is paramount that it be so, because there are hardly any villages for “indios” in which most people are not Spanish *vecinos* or people of color inhabiting the lands of *resguardos* or their surroundings. If they are to be free, there will be no villages or sources of tribute, or in any case earnings will be very narrow. In this regard, I think that Your Majesty is better off, and the government would benefit, if *indios* were to become Spanish and in this way erase all memory of their tribute and the natural aversion that commands them. […]

> “From these principles Your Excellency will gather the critical state of the population of the district and of the whole real audiencia: after the conquest, there were many villages for “indios” and few Spanish settlements, and despite the laws that prohibited it, they started intermixing with them and their children and descendants were mixed with white, mestizo, black, and mulatto, and their different propagations have formed the largest group of which the population is composed today. In this way, villages for “indios” were transformed into parishes of Spanish people, that is, of *vecinos*, who are not pure *indios*, and separating them completely is so difficult that it is only ever applied to the ones causing express harm.”

> — Francisco Antonio Moreno y Escandón, 1778.

title: Laws for the Dissolution of Resguardos
definition:
**Decree of September 24th, 1810**

> Second Article. “In accordance with the referred levelling and awarding of citizenship to *indios* with the full restitution of the rights they will start to exercise, they will be awarded ownership over lands from their *resguardos*, distributed in each village according to their fair value and in different degrees in proportion to their families so they may enjoy them and benefit from all their natural and industrial production, with the sole condition that, for the moment, they may not sell, donate, or rid themselves in any other way of the portion of land they received for a period of twenty years during which they will grow attached to the land and skilled in its administration so that it will not be easy to trick or reduce them by abusing their natural simplicity, and dispossess them of their property. They may also dispose of their lands for the benefit of their children according to the laws of the kingdom, and may pay dowry for their daughters when they marry maintaining just and right proportions, without harming their other descendants.”

title: Political Constitution of Colombia, 1991
definition:
> Article 21. “Legal nature. Native *resguardos* are the collective property of indigenous communities and they are constituted in their favor. Following articles 63 and 329 of the Political Constitution, they are unalienable, imprescriptible, and cannot be seized.

> “Resguardos are a legal and sociopolitical institution of special characteristics, formed by one or more indigenous communities with collective property titles that enjoy the guarantees of private property, inasmuch as they possess their territory. The body that controls the administration of the territory and of the life of its inhabitants is an autonomous organization protected by indigenous privilege and a normative system of its own.”
